data.title: Public Code Repositories Disclose Internal Tooling
data.summary:
Repositories belonging to the organisation and to its staff disclose internal hostnames,
build pipelines, dependency inventories and operational detail, independently of whether
any credential was committed.
data.description:
The credential in a repository is the finding everyone looks for. The more durable
exposure is the surrounding detail: internal naming conventions, environment variables that
name hosts, pipeline definitions that describe how deployment works, and dependency files
that disclose exactly which versions are running.

Personal accounts are the harder half of this. Staff publish work-adjacent code under their
own names, often without intending it to describe an employer's environment, and the
organisation has no administrative visibility of those accounts at all.

Commit history matters as much as current content. A file corrected in a later commit is
still present in the history, and most review processes look only at the working tree.
data.recommendation:
* Search both organisational and staff-associated repositories, including full commit
  history rather than current contents.
* Define what may be published — configuration shape, hostnames, pipeline detail — and make
  it part of engineering onboarding rather than a policy document.
* Where internal detail is already public, treat the hostnames and versions as known and
  prioritise hardening them rather than attempting removal alone.
data.short_recommendation: Search staff and org repositories including history; define what may be published.
